newsitem.title: USA: Most Cusiana Sep loadings delayed 2-5 days-traders.
newsitem.headline: Most Cusiana Sep loadings delayed 2-5 days-traders.

text.p: Most September loadings of Colombian Cusiana crude oil are expected to fall behind by two to five days because of operational tie-ups as the field ramps up production, traders said on Monday.
"It looks as though probably most of September will be affected. Not the first part, but probably the back two-thirds," a trader familiar with operator British Petroleum Co Plc's plans said.
Despite the delays, the three companies that market Cusiana, Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol, BP and France's Total SA, are not expected to declare force majeure on the affected cargoes.
BP, which operates the giant Cusiana/Cupiagua complex in the Andean foothills, declined to comment.
Ecopetrol officials were not immediately available for comment.

The original September program, which consists of 15 cargoes, including a cross-month shipment loading September 29 to October 3, marked a sharp increase from the August line-up of 10 cargoes and a July average of seven.
Most of the September cargoes have already been sold to U.S. refiners. Two cargoes, a BP shipment loading September 19-23 and a Total cargo loading September 23-27, were still looking for buyers.
It was unclear whether Ecopetrol was still offering a September 25-29 cargo or whether that shipment would be shifted into the October program.

A flurry of Cusiana deals last week reinforced the grade's strong appeal among U.S. refiners. The gasoline-rich crude changed hands several times between $1.05 and $1.10 a barrel under benchmark October West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.
Sellers were now asking 85-90 cents under November WTI, partly reflecting the absence of competing North Sea barrels in the Gulf, traders said.
The expected delays seem to reflect a one-month setback in the scheduled ramp-up of Cusiana production, which is now running around 215,000 barrels per day (bpd).
A target of 320,000 bpd that was supposed to be reached at the end of July or early August was pushed back to late August or early September.
Similarly, a peak of 500,000 bpd was pushed back to late January or early February from a late-December-early January target.
Threats against contract workers from leftist rebels caused a one-month delay in construction work in June.
BP, however, has saidthe delay was a result of the need for further testing on the new Ocensa pipeline that carries Cusiana crude to the Caribbean port of Coveqas.
